Volume 09 · Chapter 05

Arbitrage, state prices and discount factors

Advanced Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v09-c04

By the endPrice contingent payoffs using no-arbitrage and stochastic discount-factor reasoning.

Price the same dated payoff consistently

Capability. Replicate contingent payoffs, construct arbitrage trades from inconsistent quotes, prove the finite-state connection between no arbitrage and positive state prices, and use a stochastic discount factor without confusing it with a probability. The prerequisite is CAPM and equilibrium risk pricing. We also use linear systems and rank, orthogonal projection, compactness and attained minima, and covariance and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.

A dealer offers a contingent payment for 34 currency units. Another desk can assemble exactly that payment for 33.6. Before saying “arbitrage,” identify each security, each dated cash flow, whether a short sale is permitted, and how the initial receipt is invested. If the payment cannot be assembled, a single fair value may require assumptions beyond no arbitrage. This chapter develops both situations in a fully specified finite market.

All numerical markets below are original and synthetic. They have one currency, CU, and dates 0 and 1. There is no interim trading, dividend, tax, transaction cost, margin call or default. A stock payoff includes all terminal proceeds. Unrestricted positive and negative real holdings can be bought at the same quoted price. These are substantive model assumptions. Later chapters examine the funding, execution and information frictions that can prevent an apparent price discrepancy from being a feasible arbitrage.

1. Payoffs, prices and the exact meaning of arbitrage

There are S possible states at date 1. Each has physical probability πs > 0, with Σπs = 1. Physical probabilities describe the model's distribution of outcomes. States declared impossible should be removed before applying a theorem about positive probability gains. There are N traded assets. The matrix X has S rows and N columns; Xsj is asset j's terminal payoff in state s. Its date-0 price is pj. A vector h of asset quantities costs pᵀh and pays Xh. Quantities can be negative and need not sum to one; they are not portfolio wealth weights.

One asset is a default-free unit-payoff bond: its column is the vector 1 and its price is B > 0. Its gross safe return is Rf = 1/B; its simple return is rf = Rf − 1. Earlier chapters used R for simple risky returns. Here we preserve that convention and write a positive-price asset's gross return as G = 1 + R = X/p. A zero-cost trade has a payoff but cannot acquire a return by division by zero. A negative price is meaningful for some signed claims, although it is not a positive investment denominator.

An arbitrage is a permitted h with pᵀh ≤ 0 and Xh ≥ 0 state by state, with either a strictly negative initial cost or at least one strictly positive terminal payoff. Positive physical probabilities make a nonzero nonnegative payoff a gain with positive probability. The bond lets us restate the definition using zero initial cost: if pᵀh < 0, buy −pᵀh/B additional bonds with the receipt. The adjusted position costs zero and adds a positive payment in every state. Thus no arbitrage is equivalent to there being no nonzero nonnegative payoff obtainable at zero cost.

The law of one price says that two permitted portfolios with identical state-by-state payoffs have the same cost. Otherwise buy the cheaper and short the dearer; their future payments cancel and the initial receipt can be banked. This proves that no arbitrage implies the law. It also makes the price of a replicable payoff H well defined: if Xh = H, then P(H) = pᵀh is independent of which replica h was chosen. Additivity and homogeneity follow by adding and scaling portfolios, so P is a linear function on the span of X's columns. Linearity alone does not ensure that a positive payoff has a positive price; Exercise 3 separates those concepts.

Worked example 1 — Aster's replica and an executable model certificate

The Aster State Claims market has the following three terminal states. Prices are per unit at date 0; the call has strike 100 and pays max(stock payoff − 100, 0).

Aster's original synthetic dated claims
ItemLowMiddleHighDate-0 price
Physical probability π1/51/23/10Not a price
Unit bond11124/25 = 0.96
Stock6010014096
Call004048/5 = 9.6
Claim H103070Quote to audit: 34

Let (a,b,c) be bond, stock and call units replicating H. The first two states give a + 60b = 10 and a + 100b = 30, hence b = 1/2 and a = −20. The high state requires −20 + 140/2 + 40c = 70, so c = 1/2. The negative bond quantity is borrowing with a specified terminal repayment. The replica's price is

−20(24/25) + (1/2)96 + (1/2)(48/5) = 168/5 = 33.6.

At the separate quote 34, buy this replica and short one H. The date-0 cost is −0.4 and all three terminal net payments are zero. Invest the 0.4 receipt in 0.4/0.96 = 5/12 additional bonds. The full zero-cost trade has quantities (−235/12, 1/2, 1/2) in the original assets and −1 in H; it pays 5/12 CU in every state. This is a complete arbitrage certificate under the stated trading rules. Merely observing that one expected return exceeds another would not supply such a certificate.

If the claim quote were below 33.6, reverse the claim-versus-replica position and bank the receipt. At 33.6 there is no receipt. The amount available to cover any real execution or funding cost is the dated difference, not an unspecified “risk-free profit.” If shorting H is unavailable, the displayed high-quote trade is outside the assumed feasible set and its conclusion cannot be transferred unchanged.

2. State prices and a finite fundamental theorem

An Arrow or unit state claim pays 1 CU in a specified state and zero elsewhere. A state-price vector q satisfies Xᵀq = p: each traded price is the sum of its state payoffs weighted by q. Where an Arrow claim is replicable, qs is its actual replication price. In an incomplete market some Arrow claims are unavailable; a q then extends the observed price rule to untraded payoffs. Extensions need not be unique. The bond equation requires 1ᵀq = B.

Finite-state pricing theorem. Under the market and unrestricted-trading assumptions above, there is no arbitrage if and only if there exists q with every qs > 0 and Xᵀq = p. Strict positivity is essential; a zero price for a replicable positive state claim permits a free gain. The result establishes existence of a positive pricing rule, not a particular investor's preferences or a physical probability law.

Sufficiency. Suppose q > 0 prices every asset. For any h, pᵀh = qᵀXh. If Xh is nonnegative and nonzero, this value is strictly positive, so h cannot be an arbitrage. If Xh = 0 its cost is zero, which also rules out a negative-cost zero-payoff trade. This checks both parts of the definition.

Necessity, with the separation step proved. For each asset form the financed payoff dj = Xj − (pj/B)1. It costs zero: buy the asset and sell pj/B bonds. Let L be the linear span of these dj. This is exactly the set of zero-cost payoffs. Every linear combination is financed at zero cost; conversely a portfolio h with pᵀh = 0 has Xh = Σhjdj. No arbitrage therefore means L contains no nonzero nonnegative vector.

Take the probability simplex D = {z ≥ 0 : 1ᵀz = 1}. It is compact, is disjoint from L, and contains each coordinate unit vector es. Let PL be Euclidean orthogonal projection onto the finite-dimensional subspace L. The continuous function f(z) = (1/2)‖z − PLz‖² attains its minimum on D at z*. Its minimum is positive: a zero would put z* in L ∩ D. Define d = z* − PLz*. Then d is nonzero and orthogonal to L.

For any z in D, the segment z* + t(z − z*) stays in D for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1. Since f is minimized at t = 0, its right derivative there is nonnegative: dᵀ(z − z*) ≥ 0. Orthogonality gives dᵀz* = ‖d‖². Setting z = es therefore yields ds ≥ ‖d‖² > 0 in every state. Normalize q = Bd/(1ᵀd). Then q > 0, 1ᵀq = B and qᵀdj = 0. Expanding the last equality gives qᵀXj = pj. That proves necessity without assuming that the market already contains all Arrow claims.

Brunnermeier's Princeton one-period pricing lecture is a primary teaching route for state prices, the finite no-arbitrage theorem and completeness. The projection argument here makes the strict-positivity step explicit. Infinite-state or continuous-time versions need additional topological and trading conditions; this finite proof does not establish those versions.

Worked example 2 — Solve for q and test its sign

In Aster, the call equation is 40qhigh = 9.6, so qhigh = 0.24. Subtracting 100 times the bond equation from the stock equation gives −40qlow + 40qhigh = 0, so qlow = 0.24 and qmiddle = 0.48. Hence

q = (6/25,12/25,6/25),   Σq = 24/25 = B.

Every component is positive, certifying no arbitrage in the three-asset market. Pricing H directly gives 0.24(10) + 0.48(30) + 0.24(70) = 33.6, agreeing with replication. Its physical expected payoff is 0.2(10) + 0.5(30) + 0.3(70) = 38; discounting that mean at the safe rate gives 36.48, which is not its replication value. Probability and state value perform different jobs.

Now change only the call quote to 24. The unique vector becomes (0.6, −0.24, 0.6). This complete market prices the middle-state Arrow claim negatively. Its replica is (−3/2, 1/40, −1/20): direct substitution gives (0,1,0), while its date-0 cost at the altered call quote is −0.24. Add 1/4 bond with the receipt. The resulting portfolio (−5/4,1/40,−1/20) costs zero and pays (1/4,5/4,1/4). A negative weight in a pricing solution has become a dated trade, not merely a warning in a spreadsheet.

This inference uses uniqueness here. In an incomplete market, finding one solution with a negative component does not prove arbitrage if another solution is strictly positive. The theorem asks whether a positive solution exists. Exercise 8 makes that distinction decisive.

3. Completeness, uniqueness and what remains unidentified

A market is complete if every H in ℝS can be replicated: span(X) = ℝS, or rank(X) = S. The number of securities alone does not decide this; redundant columns add no new payoff direction. Under no arbitrage, completeness is equivalent to uniqueness of q. If X has rank S, its transpose has no nonzero null vector, so two solutions of Xᵀq = p must coincide. Conversely, if rank(X) < S, take nonzero v with Xᵀv = 0. Starting from any positive q, choose ε > 0 small enough that ε|vs| < qs wherever vs ≠ 0. Both q + εv and q − εv remain strictly positive and price all traded assets. Thus q is not unique.

Aster's three-by-three matrix has determinant 40² = 1,600, so it is complete. Removing the call leaves rank two and makes the market incomplete. Adding a fourth asset equal to two stocks does not make the original complete market “more complete.” At its consistent price 192 it creates redundant holdings: buying two stocks or that fourth asset gives the same payoff. State prices remain unique, while the representation of a payoff by asset quantities need not be. Uniqueness of prices and uniqueness of portfolios are different rank questions.

A sharper statement identifies which claims have unique no-arbitrage values even in an incomplete market. If H = Xh, every compatible q gives qᵀH = pᵀh. If H is outside span(X), project it onto that span and let v = H − Pspan(X)H. Then Xᵀv = 0 and vᵀH = ‖v‖² > 0. The positive perturbations q ± εv constructed above price H differently. Therefore a claim has a unique value across all positive extensions exactly when it is replicable. This is an identification result under unrestricted finite-state pricing; one chosen utility model can select an extension, but no arbitrage alone has not selected it.

Hedging gives useful bounds. If a replicable L satisfies L ≤ H, a quote for H below P(L) lets us buy H and short L with an initial receipt and nonnegative future payoff. A replicable U ≥ H similarly rules out quotes above P(U). Equality can also be excluded when the hedge differs from H by a nonzero nonnegative payoff. Whether a general bound is strict depends on that difference, attainable hedges and the exact market; the next case proves its own endpoints.

Worked example 3 — A digital claim that the stock and bond cannot span

Remove Aster's call but retain the bond and stock quotes. Their two equations imply qlow = qhigh = t and qmiddle = 24/25 − 2t. Strict positivity gives

q(t) = (t,24/25 − 2t,t),   0 < t < 12/25.

The high-state digital D = (0,0,1) is not affine in the stock payoff, so it cannot be replicated with these two assets. Its possible no-arbitrage price is t. For example, quotes 4/25 and 8/25 produce positive q vectors (4/25,16/25,4/25) and (8/25,8/25,8/25), respectively. Each extended three-asset market has no arbitrage, although the new digital prices differ. No physical probability calculation has forced one to be chosen.

The zero payoff is a subhedge with cost zero. A superhedge is U = (stock − 60 bonds)/80, whose payoffs are (0,1/2,1) and cost is (96 − 60×0.96)/80 = 12/25. At a digital quote zero, buy it for free: its payoff is nonzero and nonnegative. At a quote 12/25, buy U and short D for zero cost: the remaining payoff is (0,1/2,0). Both endpoints are arbitrages, so the admissible interval is open. Beyond an endpoint, the same position also produces an initial receipt that can be banked.

This incompleteness does not make all prices indeterminate. The affine claim A = (20,40,60) equals half a stock minus ten unit bonds, and has the unique value 38.4. Adding the original call restores completeness and fixes the digital at 9.6/40 = 0.24. Its price was learned from a new traded payoff, not from fitting the missing physical probability.

4. One stochastic discount factor prices every traded payoff

For any positive q and physical probabilities π > 0 define the stochastic discount factor, or pricing kernel, by ms = qs/πs. Then for every traded or consistently replicated claim,

p = ΣqsXs = Eπ[mX],   Eπ[m] = B = 1/Rf.
For a positive-price claim: 1 = Eπ[mG].
For an excess payoff G − Rf: Eπ[m(G − Rf)] = 0.

The same m enters each asset's price; the state covariance with each payoff supplies the different adjustment. m is positive but is not generally at most one, and its components need not sum to one. The deterministic bond discount B is its physical expectation. If physical probabilities change while q and the traded payoffs/prices stay fixed, the representation m = q/π changes. Completeness fixes q; it fixes m only relative to a specified physical probability law.

Normalize q instead to obtain risk-neutral probabilities Qs = qs/B = Rfqs. These are positive and sum to one. Algebra gives p = B EQ[X] and EQ[G] = Rf. “Risk neutral” names this pricing representation; it does not show that actual investors are risk neutral or that Q predicts state frequencies. For a single date-0 information set this is ordinary finite expectation. At later decision dates the analogous equations use probabilities and expectations conditional on the information available then.

Expanding the fundamental equation into mean and covariance gives

p = E[m]E[X] + Cov(m,X),
E[G] − Rf = −Cov(m,G)/E[m].

A payoff that arrives in high-m states has a larger price than safe discounting of the same physical mean; its expected return is lower. A high expected return compensates negative covariance with m in this representation. Large standalone variance need not command a premium. Zero covariance with m implies zero excess mean, even for a variable payoff. A regression residual orthogonal to some selected factor is not automatically orthogonal to the true pricing kernel; that distinction leads into factor pricing.

For σ(G) > 0, Cauchy–Schwarz yields the exact population bound

|E[G] − Rf|/σ(G) ≤ σ(m)/E[m].

This follows by substituting |Cov(m,G)| ≤ σ(m)σ(G) into the preceding identity. If both standard deviations are positive, equality requires the centered return to be proportional to centered m; a positive excess mean requires a negative proportionality coefficient. If m is constant, every priced return has zero expected excess return. If a positive-price payoff has zero variance, positive probabilities make it constant in every state and no arbitrage forces its gross return to equal Rf. For a zero-cost payoff Y, use E[mY] = 0 to obtain E[Y] = −Cov(m,Y)/E[m] and the same mean-to-standard-deviation bound in payoff units. Do not call Y a return on zero equity.

The bound restricts moments of correctly priced payoffs, but it does not make every point satisfying the inequality attainable from a given incomplete asset menu. Nor does an estimated sample ratio above a proposed bound, by itself, constitute a sure-payoff arbitrage: the pricing model, probability estimates, measurement and sample uncertainty also need examination.

Worked example 4 — The pricing weights stay fixed while beliefs change

Using Aster's complete-market q and original π gives m = (6/5,24/25,4/5) = (1.2,0.96,0.8). Its mean is 0.2(1.2) + 0.5(0.96) + 0.3(0.8) = 0.96, and Q = (1/4,1/2,1/4). The stock's physical expected payoff is 104, so E[G] = 104/96 = 13/12. The safe gross return is 25/24. Therefore the simple expected stock return is 1/12 and its expected excess return is 1/24.

Direct multiplication gives E[mG] = 1. Hence Cov(m,G) = 1 − (24/25)(13/12) = −1/25, and −Cov(m,G)/E[m] = 1/24 as required. The financed stock payoff per one initial CU is G − Rf = (−5/12,0,5/12). Its positive expected value is compatible with a loss in the low state, so it is not an arbitrage. The units and full payoff vector settle the question.

Now replace the physical probabilities by π̃ = (3/10,1/2,1/5), holding all prices and payoffs fixed. Then m̃ = (4/5,24/25,6/5); Q and q are unchanged. The expected stock payoff becomes 96, its expected gross return becomes 1, and its expected excess return becomes −1/24. Covπ̃(m̃,G) = 1/25 makes the pricing identity hold again. No arbitrage did not determine which physical law was correct. It determined relationships among prices of state-contingent payments.

For the original law, Var(G) = 49/576, so σ(G) = 7/24 and the stock's Sharpe ratio is 1/7. Var(m) = 12/625, giving [σ(m)/E[m]]² = 1/48. The squared stock ratio is 1/49 < 1/48. Both are population quantities of this invented market, not estimates of a trading opportunity. Exercise 6 constructs a replicable unit-cost payoff achieving equality and explains the required covariance sign.

5. A marginal-utility interpretation, with its conditions

One economic model can explain why payments in some states receive higher weight. Suppose an investor values u(c0) + δΣπsu(cs), with δ > 0, differentiable increasing concave u, and positive current and future consumption at the candidate optimum. Buying a small quantity θ of a claim priced p changes consumption to c0 − θp and cs + θXs. Assume both positive and negative sufficiently small θ are feasible. Differentiating at an interior optimum gives

−p u′(c0) + δΣπsu′(cs)Xs = 0,
p = E[mX],   ms = δu′(cs)/u′(c0) > 0.

Under concavity, vanishing derivatives for all feasible unrestricted directions also support optimality on the convex positive-consumption budget set. Low consumption tends to make marginal utility high, so a claim paying in those states can provide valuable insurance. But the Euler equation by itself has not solved for consumption, endowments, aggregate resources or market clearing. In incomplete markets different investors can agree on traded prices while their marginal-utility kernels differ on directions the securities do not span.

A borrowing limit, shorting restriction or boundary consumption choice can prevent a two-sided derivative argument. If only θ ≥ 0 is feasible at θ = 0, optimality requires the right derivative to be nonpositive: E[mX] ≤ p. The equality need not hold for that investor's constrained decision. This does not authorize applying the unrestricted finite-market theorem to a different feasible-trade set.

Cochrane's author-hosted sample chapters, Chapter 1, provide a primary route to the consumption Euler equation and SDF notation. We use an original finite construction and separate the marginal condition from a solved equilibrium. Our symbol G denotes the gross return; the source uses a different return convention.

6. Reproduce, perturb and distinguish a theorem from its application

The synthetic inputs, standard-library program, full reference output, file manifest and execution guide form the offline Aster laboratory. Exact fractions preserve every budget, state price and covariance equality. The program reports actual asset quantities for inconsistent quotes, including the bond bought with the initial receipt. It removes the call before computing incomplete-market bounds, then adds a digital at each experimental quote and checks the resulting extended market.

The named fixture permits three positive, equally spaced stock payoffs with the call struck at the middle payoff. The README states its strict domain, its rejection of contradictory policies and how to inspect bad quotes in separate diagnostic fields. Changing probabilities changes m and physical return moments; changing a payoff or price changes the corresponding replication calculation. The full output also constructs positive log-utility consumption and a bound-attaining payoff. Those are disclosed mathematical constructions, not fitted preferences, observed data or demonstrations that a real institution can finance the trades.

A reliable price audit records the payoff definition, currency, settlement time, feasible positions, source of the physical distribution, rank of the traded payoff matrix, sign of the pricing rule and every dated cash flow of any proposed arbitrage. If the claim is outside the traded span, report what no arbitrage actually identifies and which additional model selects a point within that set. Replication, an economic equilibrium and a statistical forecast answer related but distinct questions.

Exercises

  1. A new claim and reversed trade. In the original complete Aster market, replicate H₁ = (8,20,52), price it by both holdings and q, and construct a zero-cost arbitrage if it is quoted at 23. State the short position and every terminal net payoff.
  2. All three unit state claims. Derive bond/stock/call replicas of (1,0,0), (0,1,0) and (0,0,1). Price them under the original quotes. Then replace the call quote by 24 and by 0, separately. For each altered market give a zero-cost arbitrage. Explain why a nonnegative q with zero components is insufficient.
  3. Prove the missing logical steps. In the finite theorem prove that the financed columns span exactly the zero-cost payoffs, explain why the minimum over D is positive, and derive ds > 0 from the directional derivative. Separately consider two states, a unit bond priced 1, and a stock paying (0,2) priced 3. Show that the law of one price holds but no arbitrage fails; give an explicit zero-cost trade.
  4. Incomplete does not mean unpriced. Remove Aster's call. List all compatible positive q and the high-state digital price interval. Audit a digital quote 9/25 and both endpoints. Price A = (20,40,60) uniquely. Explain why adding a security equal to two stocks at price 192 does not identify the digital price.
  5. Probability versus price. Compute m, Q, the stock expected simple return, and Cov(m,G) under each physical law in Worked example 4. Verify all three traded prices using E[mX]. A colleague uses the original π as risk-neutral probabilities and reports stock price 99.84. Identify the failed equality and explain why q itself is not a probability distribution here.
  6. A tight discount-factor bound. Under original Aster probabilities, verify Var(m) = 12/625, Var(G) = 49/576 and the squared Sharpe comparison. Prove that G* = Rf + E[m²]/E[m] − m costs one. Find its three state values, bond/stock/call replica, mean excess payoff and variance. Show equality in the bound and explain why this construction is tradeable in this market.
  7. Euler equality or inequality. Let u(c) = log c, δ = 24/25, c0 = 1 and future consumption (4/5,1,6/5), with original Aster probabilities. Derive its kernel and marginal valuation of H = (10,30,70). If an additional purchase of H is buy-only at quote 34 and zero units are held, evaluate the right derivative of utility and the appropriate boundary inequality. Explain what remains unproved about equilibrium.
  8. Audit a pricing memo. For the incomplete bond/stock market an analyst finds q̂ = (3/5,−6/25,3/5), observes Xᵀq̂ = p, and writes: “A negative state price proves this market has arbitrage; our estimate therefore uniquely prices the untraded middle-state digital at −0.24. We can buy it now and safely hold to maturity despite unspecified funding constraints.” Evaluate each inference. Supply a positive compatible vector and a concrete account of what changes if the middle-state digital really becomes tradable at that negative quote. Grade the claim using mathematical existence, identification and feasible cash flows.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria
  1. Replica and purchase. The low/middle difference gives stock units (20 − 8)/40 = 3/10. Bond units are 8 − 60(3/10) = −10. The high state then has −10 + 140(3/10) = 32, so call units are (52 − 32)/40 = 1/2. Cost is −9.6 + 28.8 + 4.8 = 24; qᵀH₁ = 0.24(8) + 0.48(20) + 0.24(52) = 24. Buy H₁ at 23 and short its replica: original-asset quantities (10,−3/10,−1/2). This costs −1 and has zero terminal payoff. Buy 25/24 extra bonds with the receipt, so final original-asset quantities are (265/24,−3/10,−1/2), plus one H₁. Initial cost is zero and each terminal payoff is 25/24. The short stock/call positions and permitted signed bond trade must be stated; expected-profit language alone is insufficient.
  2. Arrow basis. In bond/stock/call units the low replica is (5/2,−1/40,1/40), the middle is (−3/2,1/40,−1/20), and the high is (0,0,1/40). Substitution into all three rows verifies their payoffs. Original costs are 6/25,12/25,6/25. At call price 24 these become (3/5,−6/25,3/5). Buy the middle replica and 1/4 extra bond: (−5/4,1/40,−1/20), cost zero, payoffs (1/4,5/4,1/4). At call price zero, buy 1/40 call for zero cost and receive (0,0,1). The corresponding q = (0,24/25,0) is nonnegative but assigns zero value to a positive-probability attainable gain. Weak nonnegativity thus misses this arbitrage under our definition.
  3. Proof and counterexample. A coefficient vector h applied to dj produces Xh − (pᵀh/B)1, implementable by h plus a financing bond position. Conversely pᵀh = 0 makes Xh equal that combination. The continuous squared distance attains a minimum on compact D. If it were zero, the minimizer would lie in L and D, contradicting no arbitrage; the finite-dimensional subspace is closed and its orthogonal projection exists. For z = es, the feasible segment's right derivative is dᵀ(es − z*) ≥ 0, while dᵀz* = ‖d‖² > 0, so ds ≥ ‖d‖² > 0. Normalize by the positive sum to obtain q and check each asset equation. In the separate two-state example the payoff matrix [[1,0],[1,2]] is invertible, so each payoff has unique holdings and the price functional satisfies the law of one price. But q = (−1/2,3/2). Buy two bonds and short a stock: cost −1, payoff (2,0). Invest the receipt in one further bond; three bonds minus one stock cost zero and pay (3,1). Full credit requires both the proof's strict inequality and the explicit distinction between a linear rule and a positive rule.
  4. A family and a fixed value. The family is (t,24/25 − 2t,t), 0 < t < 12/25. At t = 9/25 the vector is (9/25,6/25,9/25), strictly positive, so the extended market is arbitrage free. At zero buy the digital; at 12/25 buy (stock − 60 bonds)/80 and short the digital, leaving (0,1/2,0) for zero cost. A is half a stock minus ten bonds and costs 192/5 = 38.4 under every positive q. Two stocks at price 192 adds a redundant column and price equation, so the rank stays two and t remains unidentified. Merely increasing the count of listed assets is insufficient.
  5. Two representations of the same prices. Original m = (6/5,24/25,4/5), alternative m̃ = (4/5,24/25,6/5), and Q = (1/4,1/2,1/4) in both cases. E[m] = Ẽ[m̃] = 24/25. Expected simple stock returns are 1/12 and 0; covariances with G are −1/25 and +1/25. In either law πsms = qs, so E[m×bond] = 24/25, E[m×stock] = 0.24(60) + 0.48(100) + 0.24(140) = 96, and E[m×call] = 0.24(40) = 48/5. Using π as Q produces B Eπ[stock] = (24/25)104 = 99.84, inconsistent with observed price 96 and replication. It omits the nonzero covariance adjustment. q sums to 0.96, while Q sums to one. Neither normalizing q nor computing m determines the correct physical frequencies.
  6. Equality is constructible here. Centered m is (6/25,0,−4/25), giving variance (1/5)(36/625) + (3/10)(16/625) = 12/625. Stock payoff variance is (1/5)44² + (1/2)4² + (3/10)36² = 784, so return variance is 784/96² = 49/576. Its premium is 1/24, hence squared Sharpe ratio 1/49, below (12/625)/(24/25)² = 1/48. Also E[m²] = (24/25)² + 12/625 = 588/625, and E[m²]/E[m] = 49/50. Since RfE[m] = 1, E[mG*] = 1 + E[m²] − E[m²] = 1. State values are (493,637,733)/600. Their replica is (277/600,3/500,−1/500); cost is 277/625 + 72/125 − 12/625 = 1. Expected excess payoff is 49/50 − 24/25 = 1/50, variance is 12/625, and their squared ratio is 1/48. The centered payoff is exactly −(m − E[m]), so correlation is −1. Completeness supplies the replica, and unrestricted signed quantities permit its short call. In a different incomplete or constrained market the algebraic payoff need not be attainable.
  7. Preference interpretation with a boundary. Since u′(c) = 1/c, ms = δc0/cs, giving (6/5,24/25,4/5). The marginal valuation of H is qᵀH = 168/5 = 33.6. At quote 34 the derivative of u(1 − 34θ) + δΣπslog(cs + θHs) at zero is −34 + 33.6 = −2/5. For θ ≥ 0 the nonpositive right derivative satisfies the boundary condition E[mH] ≤ 34; concavity supports choosing no additional purchase along this feasible direction. If a two-sided small trade were allowed, the negative derivative would make a small sale desirable and zero would not be an interior optimum. This calculation has not specified aggregate endowments, all investors, supply or clearing, and therefore has not established an economy-wide equilibrium or an empirical consumption model.
  8. Existence, identification and implementation. The proposed q̂ sums to 24/25 and values the stock at (3/5)60 − (6/25)100 + (3/5)140 = 96, so it is a linear extension of the two observed prices. Its negative middle component prevents that extension from being positive. It does not rule out the positive vector (6/25,12/25,6/25), which prices the same assets and certifies no arbitrage in the original market. A middle-state digital is not affine in (60,100,140), so its value is not identified by those two quotes. Across positive extensions its price is 24/25 − 2t, spanning (0,24/25). The negative “estimate” is neither unique nor a valid positive extension. If the digital is actually available at −6/25 with unrestricted settlement, buying one gives an initial receipt 6/25. Invest it in 1/4 bond, yielding a zero-cost trade with payoffs (1/4,5/4,1/4). Without actual availability there is no such trade; with unspecified restrictions its feasibility has not been shown. Grade equally on these three domains: existence of a positive extension rather than one solver's sign; identification versus an extra model choice; and a dated, permitted position rather than a verbal holding claim. A correct memo supplies the repaired conclusion and names any missing contract or funding information.

Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain to a colleague why q, π and m are three different objects. Use one state to state their units or role, show which sums to one, and derive p = E[mX] without saying that a risk-neutral probability is the actual likelihood. Then explain why the same stock/bond prices can support several digital quotes when the call is absent.

Delayed check. After several days, reconstruct the Aster state prices and the finite theorem's positive separating vector without opening the solution. Price a claim paying (2,6,14), decide whether the digital quote 0.50 is admissible without the call, and state why one negative incomplete-market pricing solution proves less than a negative unique complete-market solution.

Retention benchmark

State prices are (0.24,0.48,0.24). The claim is one fifth of H, so its price is 6.72 and replica is (−4,1/10,1/10). With only stock and bond the digital upper bound is 0.48. At quote 0.50, buy the superhedge and short the digital, bank 0.02 in 1/48 bond, and obtain zero initial cost with payoffs (1/48,25/48,1/48). For the proof reconstruct the minimum squared distance from D to L and derive ds ≥ ‖d‖² > 0 before normalizing. Incompleteness requires searching for the existence of a positive extension; completeness makes the unique solution decisive.

Sources and further study

The inspected sections of Brunnermeier's one-period lecture cover price functionals, positive state prices, completeness and the change of probability representation. The original Aster market and projection proof use their own notation, derivations and problems.

The inspected Cochrane sample PDF carries a 2001 copyright and supplies Chapter 1's Euler-equation, payoff/return and covariance-pricing route. Its historical empirical discussions are not evidence for this synthetic case. The next chapter develops exact and approximate factor pricing, including when factor-orthogonal residual risk can still be priced. Dynamic trading, derivative replication and continuous-time extensions belong to the planned quantitative-finance volume; this chapter's finite theorem is complete within its stated domain.

Sources and further study

  • Markus K. Brunnermeier — FIN 501 Lecture 03: One-Period Model, Pricing — Primary teaching route for linear payoff pricing, strictly positive finite-state prices, completeness and risk-neutral/SDF representations. Aster examples, exercises and the projection proof are original.
  • John H. Cochrane — Asset Pricing, author-hosted sample chapters (copy carrying 2001 copyright) — Primary author route for the consumption marginal-utility Euler equation, stochastic discount factor, return/payoff conventions, covariance pricing and the Cauchy bound. Original finite examples separate no-arbitrage, preference interpretation and a solved equilibrium.
